title: When Can We Stop Talking About Trump?
text:

The Conversation
When Can We Stop Talking About Trump?
Frank Bruni: Bret, I’m utterly fascinated and deeply amused by all the efforts over the past week to read President Trump’s post-midterms mood and project exactly how he’ll quack and precisely how he’ll waddle as he dons the sad feathers of a lame duck. I mean, we’re talking about Trump here. He’s erratic and incoherent on his most triumphant days. What do you think we can expect from him in sweeping, mortifying, eviscerating defeat?
Bret Stephens: His choice of Stephen Miller as his next chief of staff says it all: two years of bruising political combat; no outreach to Democrats; no grace in defeat; no acknowledgment of political reality; no interest in giving another Republican a fighting chance to succeed him.
Frank: So it’s all truculence all the time? Grudges galore and a permanent snit? I suppose that’s the thrust of the ludicrous letter that the chief White House counsel, Will Scharf, wrote to Representative Robert Garcia of California, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, warning him that aggressive investigations into the conduct of Trump and his aides “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” Maybe Scharf was rehearsing material for some new stand-up act? He’s certainly ignoring all the Americans whose votes made clear that they have plenty of qualms and questions about the conduct of this White House.
Bret: You know the old fable about the scorpion and the frog, Frank? Well, Trump is the scorpion and America is the frog that elected him twice. And got stung twice, too.
Frank: Will the scorpion — and Miller, who’s maybe a tarantula in this formulation — be able to do much concrete damage through executive orders and other actions that ignore and sideline Congress, or are you describing what will mostly be ugly theater? And even if it’s just ugly theater, where does that leave Americans who, I think, just begged politicians to calm down, grow up and reclaim a smidgen of dignity?
Bret: If only Miller were as docile and relatively harmless as a tarantula, Frank. Miller is going to take Barack Obama’s notorious motto from 2014, “I’ve got a pen and I’ve got a phone” — meaning that he intended to bypass a hostile Congress through executive orders — and take it to a whole new level of aggression, all of it with a view toward achieving two things: making Democrats look weak or goading them into overreaction. I don’t envy Hakeem Jeffries and … uh, whoever becomes Senate majority leader.
